title: Union Health Ministry Organises NLEP Review-cum-Capacity Building Workshop to Strengthen Leprosy Control Measures and Accelerate Interruption of Transmission
subtitle:
Workshop Brings Together Health Officials and Technical Partners to Strengthen Early Detection, Contact Tracing and Last-Mile Efforts for Interruption of Leprosy Transmission
District-Level Experience Sharing and Peer Learning Under NLEP Strengthen Early Detection, Timely Treatment and Community Engagement
body_text:
The two-day National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP) Review-cum-Capacity Building Workshop commenced today in Indore, Madhya Pradesh. Organised by the Central Leprosy Division (CLD), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, the workshop aims to strengthen programme implementation, enhance technical capacities and accelerate focused action towards achieving Interruption of Transmission (IoT) of leprosy.
The workshop brought together more than 70 participants, including the Additional Director General, Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS); Deputy Director General (Leprosy); officials of the Central Leprosy Division; representatives from RLTRI Raipur and Aska Institute; State Leprosy Officers; Chief Medical and Health Officers; District Leprosy Officers from all 51 districts of Madhya Pradesh; District Consultants; technical development partners; and a representative of APAL.
The deliberations focused on reviewing the epidemiological situation, assessing programme performance, identifying implementation gaps and sharing field-level experiences and best practices. Particular emphasis was placed on strengthening early case detection, contact tracing, timely initiation and completion of treatment, prevention of disabilities and intensified surveillance as key components of the last-mile strategy for interrupting leprosy transmission.
The workshop commenced with a welcome address by the State Leprosy Officer, Madhya Pradesh, followed by a Special Address by the Additional Director General, DGHS.
The first day of the workshop featured technical sessions focusing on the epidemiological scenario of leprosy in Madhya Pradesh, focused strategies under NLEP, improving the quality and outcomes of the Leprosy Case Detection Campaign (LCDC), and strengthening Retrospective and Reverse Contact Tracing.
The session led by Dr. Sunil V. Gitte, Deputy Director General (Leprosy), highlighted the importance of leveraging programme data to identify priority districts and areas requiring intensified surveillance and targeted interventions. Particular emphasis was laid on implementing focused strategies to bring the prevalence rate below 1 per 10,000 population, while strengthening early case detection, contact tracing, timely treatment and disability prevention as part of the last-mile efforts towards interruption of transmission.
Dr. Rashmi Shukla, National Programme Officer, WHO, led a technical session on “Improving the Quality and Outcomes of Leprosy Case Detection Campaign (LCDC)”, focusing on enhancing the quality of campaign implementation and improving the effectiveness of case detection activities.
Another technical session, conducted by Dr. Sandeep Jogdand, RLTRI Raipur, focused on “Retrospective and Reverse Contact Tracing”. The session provided technical orientation on strengthening contact-tracing approaches to identify potentially missed or undiagnosed cases and to better understand transmission dynamics within affected communities.
The technical deliberations were followed by a brainstorming and experience-sharing session with District Leprosy Officers from across Madhya Pradesh. Districts including Alirajpur, Anuppur, Barwani, Burhanpur and Dhar shared their respective field experiences, highlighting programme performance, operational challenges, priority areas and district-level actions being undertaken to strengthen early case detection, timely treatment and prevention of disability.
The experience-sharing session also facilitated peer learning among district teams and provided an opportunity to identify practical and replicable approaches for strengthening implementation. The Vice-President of APAL shared experiences and practical insights on strengthening early case detection and community-level action, underscoring the importance of incorporating the perspectives of persons affected by leprosy and enhancing community engagement in programme implementation.
The two-day workshop will continue on 20 August 2026, with further deliberations and capacity-building sessions aimed at consolidating district-level strategies, strengthening programme implementation and accelerating focused interventions towards the national goal of Interruption of Leprosy Transmission.

ministry.name: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare

enrichment.summary: The Central Leprosy Division of the Union Health Ministry held a two-day NLEP Review-cum-Capacity Building Workshop in Indore, Madhya Pradesh, starting 19 August 2026, bringing together over 70 officials from DGHS, state and district leprosy programmes, WHO, RLTRI Raipur and APAL. Sessions focused on strengthening early case detection, contact tracing, timely treatment, disability prevention and the Leprosy Case Detection Campaign to accelerate Interruption of Transmission (IoT) of leprosy. District Leprosy Officers from Madhya Pradesh shared field experiences and best practices for last-mile implementation.
enrichment.context: India declared leprosy 'eliminated' as a public health problem at the national level in 2005, defined as prevalence below 1 case per 10,000 population, under the National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP). However, elimination at the national average masked persistent pockets of high prevalence in several districts and states, and new case detection has continued, including among children, indicating ongoing transmission. The government has since shifted the programmatic goal from mere prevalence reduction to 'Interruption of Transmission' (IoT) by 2027, aligning with global efforts and the WHO's Global Leprosy Strategy. Tools like the Leprosy Case Detection Campaign (LCDC), active case finding, contact tracing (including retrospective and reverse tracing), post-exposure prophylaxis, and involvement of persons affected by leprosy (through bodies like APAL) are central to this strategy. This workshop is a routine capacity-building and review exercise for one state, reflecting the operational machinery behind the broader IoT goal rather than a new policy announcement itself.

prelims_questions.question: In the context of India's National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP), 'Interruption of Transmission' refers to which of the following?
options: Achieving zero new leprosy cases in a single calendar year across all states
Reducing prevalence rate below 1 case per 10,000 population at the national level
Breaking the chain of transmission of leprosy so that no new infections occur, as the next-stage goal after elimination
Providing free multi-drug therapy (MDT) to all diagnosed leprosy patients
prelims_questions.explanation: India achieved 'elimination' (prevalence <1/10,000) in 2005, but transmission continued; the current programmatic goal, as reiterated in the NLEP workshop, is 'Interruption of Transmission' (IoT), meaning breaking the chain of new infections, targeted for 2027.

prelims_questions.question: Which of the following is a component of the 'last-mile strategy' for interrupting leprosy transmission as discussed under NLEP?
options: Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana enrolment
National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme
prelims_questions.explanation: The release specifically mentions strengthening 'Retrospective and Reverse Contact Tracing' as a key technical strategy, along with early case detection and disability prevention, for interrupting leprosy transmission under NLEP.

mains_questions.question: Despite India achieving leprosy 'elimination' at the national level in 2005, the disease continues to be transmitted in pockets. Discuss the challenges in achieving 'Interruption of Transmission' of leprosy and suggest measures to strengthen last-mile implementation of the National Leprosy Eradication Programme.

Community participation and involvement of persons affected by a disease are often cited as critical to public health programme success. Examine this in the context of India's leprosy control efforts.

study_notes.reason: The release carries a solid factual core on NLEP's history, targets and terminology (elimination vs IoT, key institutions) alongside genuine analytical material on why national-level elimination masked persistent transmission and what last-mile strategy this requires.

prelims.point: India declared leprosy 'eliminated' as a public health problem in 2005 (prevalence below 1 per 10,000 population)
prelims.why_important: A frequently tested fact distinguishing 'elimination' (statistical threshold) from actual disease eradication.

prelims.point: National goal has shifted from prevalence reduction to 'Interruption of Transmission (IoT)' by 2027, under NLEP
prelims.why_important: Tests awareness of the programme's current phase and target year, distinct from the 2005 elimination milestone.

prelims.point: NLEP is run by the Central Leprosy Division under DGHS, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
prelims.why_important: Institutional mapping of scheme to implementing body is a common prelims distractor.

prelims.point: Leprosy Case Detection Campaign (LCDC) and Retrospective/Reverse Contact Tracing are key NLEP tools
prelims.why_important: Distinguishes specific operational mechanisms used for active case finding under NLEP.

mains.point: National-level elimination statistics can mask persistent sub-national pockets of high prevalence and continued transmission, including among children
mains.analytical_use: Useful for questions on why disease elimination declarations can be misleading and the need for disaggregated, district-level health monitoring.

mains.point: Shift from a prevalence-based target to an Interruption of Transmission goal reflects a move towards active, last-mile public health strategy
mains.analytical_use: Can support answers on evolving strategies in disease elimination programmes, e.g., comparing passive vs active surveillance models.

mains.point: Involvement of persons affected by leprosy (through APAL) highlights the value of community and stakeholder participation in last-mile implementation
mains.analytical_use: Relevant for questions on inclusive governance and the role of affected communities in policy implementation and stigma reduction.

mains.point: Persistent new case detection despite elimination indicates gaps in early detection, contact tracing and health system capacity at district level
mains.analytical_use: Useful for 'critically examine' type questions on why disease elimination targets are not always matched by transmission interruption on the ground.
